item.title: Acceptance Is Not a Trick for Feeling Good
item.description:
Trauma

Acceptance Is Not a Trick for Feeling Good

A beginner's guide to Clear Seeing.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • All emotions provide valuable information, if we listen to them.
  • Acceptance is about making space for what we're feeling.
Floodwater was waist high
Source: B Sedley

In April, my family lost our house, belongings and cat when a freak storm caused flooding. For the first few days, I felt numb. I was on autopilot just dealing with all the necessary jobs – rescuing salvageable items, throwing away other things, finding temporary accommodation and more. Most importantly, we had to help our children feel as settled as possible when nothing was settled. It felt like there was no time or space for me to have my own emotions. But anytime I paused for a minute, the emotions snuck in anyway. I felt sadness, despair, worry, shame, anger, confusion, shock and a whole lot of exhaustion.

I felt sad because we’d lost our cat and so many things we loved. Despair because I wasn’t sure how we’d bounce back from this, as well as for the state of the world when severe weather events are happening more frequently. Worry because I could see my kids really distressed. Shame because I like to help others and here I was needing to accept help from so many other people. Anger at bureaucracy that added to my stress. Confusion about what I needed to do next with lots of helpful people giving me conflicting advice. Shock because our whole life was flipped upside down overnight. Exhaustion because there was so much to do and I couldn’t think straight to do any of it. Each emotion was telling me something, but I wasn’t in a position to listen to any of it.

I’m a clinical psychologist who used Acceptance and Commitment Therapy to help people with trauma. In this series, I’m reflecting on whether the ideas I tell my clients actually helped me when my family experienced trauma.

The word ‘acceptance’ often has negative connotations. People say ‘accept it’ when they mean ‘surrender’ or ‘shut up about it already’. There can also be a worry that you’re being asked to accept something that can be changed. But that’s not what acceptance means when we use it in therapy.

Kerry Makin-Byrd, in her excellent self-help book Start Here: A Practical Guide for the Overwhelmed, describes acceptance as Clear Seeing: "When we begin by acknowledging this is what is, we stop arguing with realities that we can’t change.”

Michael J Fox, the actor who has lived with Parkinson’s Disease since he was 29, is even more direct. He has said, “Acceptance doesn't mean resignation; it means understanding that something is what it is and that there's got to be a way through it."

Both these quotes were helpful in the weeks after the flood as I learned that my only option was to take one step at a time. But even when I was doing the right steps at the right pace, I still felt the full range of uncomfortable emotions.

Acceptance for events outside my control, such as the flood, is important, but I also had to accept that I have less control of my emotions than people tell me. People tried to make me feel less sad by saying things like ‘at least you’re ok’, or ‘it could be worse’ or ‘you’ll be fine soon’. Well-meaning comments that accidentally made me feel like I’m doing something wrong when I felt sad, worried, angry, guilty, embarrassed or anything else.

So what does it mean to accept emotions? I could do all sorts of things to avoid them, like keeping so busy that there would be no time to acknowledge what I was feeling or making jokes about the situation to cover up how much of a mess I was feeling inside. I could act like everything is going to be ok so I can help my kids process it all. But the emotions didn’t go away. They just waited until I paused for a minute and then made as much noise as possible inside. My heart sank, my stomach dropped, my body felt heavy, my eyes wanted to cry (but often couldn’t).

In these moments, my mind begged me to get busy again so I wouldn’t have to feel these things. It was just doing its job of trying to protect me from discomfort. But I knew that I would encourage my clients to not avoid the feelings, but instead be more accepting. So I took in a breath and noticed that the breath could come in, pass around the sadness, and come out again. I placed a warm compassionate hand on the parts of my body that were feeling the painful emotion. There were lots of feelings that felt uncomfortable, heavy or sharp, and I noticed that I was able to hold them all. I didn’t need to fight them or fix them. I looked at each one and said 'hey, you’re here too', and let them do their job of giving me valuable information about my situation.

I frequently ask clients to try this. But when it was time for me to use it with myself, I had a million reasons why I’d be better off doing anything else other than acceptance. And yet for the sake of the people I work with, my family and for me, I took some breaths and noticed that there was room inside me for those feelings as well. It was hard and it was helpful.

What I really learned about acceptance from these past few months is that acceptance isn’t a sneaky trick. Telling myself that there’s room inside me for these feelings didn’t make them go away. Saying that I accept that I’m sad didn’t make me feel any less sad, even though I desperately hoped it would. But it did free up some of the energy I might have spent trying not to feel the feelings by avoiding, distracting, or criticizing myself. And at a time when I didn’t have much of anything, freeing up some energy was helpful.

item.title: What Makes You Unique in a Hybrid World?
item.description:
Identity

What Makes You Unique in a Hybrid World?

Psychological research highlights four ways to explore your unique identity.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI can describe behavior but can't capture lived identity or personal purpose.
  • Narrative identity integrates life stories in a way that static AI profiles cannot.
  • True passion involves sustained, voluntary investment not replaceable by algorithms.
As our tools become part of daily life, it is worth distinguishing between a mirror of behavior and an account of identity.
Source: AI-Generated

Ask an AI system who you are, and it will answer immediately, drawing on search history, purchase patterns, and other behavioral data to generate a description of your identity. The process is fast and confident, but it raises a basic question: does a generated answer actually resolve anything? As these tools become part of daily life, it is worth distinguishing between a description of behavior and an account of identity. For anyone interested in working out the answer independently, psychological research on purpose, personality, absorption in an activity, and passion offers a starting point.

Purpose: Why Are You Here?

Meaning in life is generally described in psychological research as resting on three components: significance, the sense that one's life matters; coherence, the sense that events fit into a consistent narrative; and purpose, a long-term aim that gives direction to daily activity. Michael Steger's research on meaning identifies these three components and shows that the search for meaning closely tracks identity development. Adolescents who search most actively for meaning also tend to show the clearest sense of identity; the two processes appear to develop together.

A search engine or an AI model can retrieve or generate information, but it is not oriented toward any goal beyond the immediate query. Purpose, by definition, requires a person to choose the reason behind an action. No automated system can do that on someone's behalf. In practice, this means that tools built to answer questions about purpose can surface options or precedents, but the selection of a direction remains a task for the individual.

Personality: Who Are You?

Twentieth-century personality psychology relied largely on trait measures such as the Five Factor Model: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. These measures describe broad tendencies but do not capture how a person understands their own life.

More recent research, including work by Dan McAdams and Kate McLean, treats identity as a narrative: an ongoing, revised account of one's own life that integrates past experience into a coherent sense of self. This narrative includes specific memories, decisions, and relationships that shape how a person understands who they are.

article continues after advertisement

A related concept, optimal distinctiveness theory, describes identity as a balance between the need to belong to a group and the need to be distinct from it, a balance that is continuously renegotiated over time. An AI-generated profile can reflect stated preferences, but it has no history of lived experience to draw on. Narrative identity and optimal distinctiveness both depend on an ongoing relationship between a person and their social context, which is not something a static output can replicate.

Pursuit: Where Do You Stand on Your Journey?

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's research on flow describes a state in which a person's skill level matches the demands of a task closely enough that self-consciousness and the passage of time become less noticeable. This state has been studied across many types of activity, from manual work to creative practice.

Self-determination theory, developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, adds that activities chosen for intrinsic reasons are more likely to be sustained over time than activities undertaken to meet external expectations. Autonomy is one of the theory's three basic psychological needs, alongside competence and relatedness.

Recommendation systems can suggest activities based on past behavior, but they do not participate in the sustained engagement that produces this state. That engagement depends on ongoing personal investment in a specific activity, not on a suggestion. This distinction matters for how organizations think about engagement and productivity: exposure to a task is not the same as sustained, self-directed practice in it.

Passion: What Are You Doing to Align Your Aspirations and Actions?

Robert Vallerand's dualistic model of passion distinguishes between two types of passion for an activity: harmonious passion, which is integrated into a person's identity without displacing other areas of life, and obsessive passion, which is taken up under internal or external pressure and can crowd out other priorities. Harmonious passion is generally associated with better psychological outcomes.

article continues after advertisement

Research on responses to AI-generated art provides a relevant data point. A study on anthropocentric bias found that people who believe creativity is a uniquely human trait rate AI-generated work as less creative and respond to it with more suspicion. This suggests that concerns about AI and creativity often center on the source of the work rather than its quality. In personal terms, passion depends less on the finished product than on the sustained, voluntary investment of time required to produce it.

The Common Thread

These four areas point to a consistent finding in the broader literature on meaning: people who report higher meaning in their lives also report higher self-esteem, greater self-acceptance, and more resilience under stress. Purpose, personality, pursuit and passion each contribute to this sense of meaning, and each depends on lived, ongoing personal experience that a generated output does not have access to.

A Practical Exercise to Start Your Own Inquiry

Set aside ten minutes to answer the following questions in writing, without editing for style.

1. Why am I spending time on the activity that took up the most hours this week, once external obligations are set aside?

2. Who is telling the story of my life right now, and does that account still feel accurate?

3. Where do I lose track of time, and when did I last go there intentionally?

4. What would I continue doing if there were no audience, income, or algorithm involved?

An AI system can generate plausible answers to all four questions on request. It cannot answer them from within a specific, lived life, because it has none. That distinction is where individual identity continues to reside.

item.title: The Quickest Way Out of a Negative Thought Spiral
item.description:
Self-Talk

The Quickest Way Out of a Negative Thought Spiral

The easiest way to stop spiralling does not involve working anything out.

Posted July 29, 2026

Source: Kristine Javashvili / Pexels

Most people assume a difficult mood should be understood before it can be resolved. The idea is that relief follows insight, and insight follows enough hard thinking about what went wrong. Surprisingly, the research points the other way. The most reliable way out of a negative spiral rarely begins with more thought. It begins with one small action, taken before it feels warranted.

And still, if you ask most people how to break a bad mood, they’ll describe some version of thinking their way out: sit with it, figure out why you feel this way, talk it through until it makes sense. Psychologists who study mood recovery have found something closer to the opposite works better in the moment a spiral is active. It’s called behavioral activation, and the premise is straightforward: change the behavior first, and the mood tends to follow, rather than waiting for the mood to lift before acting.

A 2021 meta-analysis published in Psychological Medicine found that behavioral activation reliably reduced both depression and anxiety symptoms compared with inactive controls, while also increasing overall activation. In practice, this means deliberately re-engaging in small, concrete activities, such as a short walk, a shower or answering one message, specifically because those actions are small enough to complete even at low motivation.

The mechanism itself is not particularly sophisticated. A five-minute task doesn’t require insight or resolve anything. It simply changes what a person’s attention and body are doing in the moment, which is often enough to loosen a loop that thought alone could not touch. Momentum, in this framework, is not the reward for feeling better; it is the mechanism that produces feeling better.

Why People Often Fail to Escape a Negative Loop

The reason this isn’t most people’s first instinct is that analyzing a bad mood feels productive. It mimics problem-solving. Psychologists have a name for what it usually is instead: rumination, or repetitive, self-focused dwelling on a negative mood.

A 2020 review published in Behaviour Research and Therapy found that rumination magnifies and prolongs negative mood, interferes with problem-solving and instrumental behavior, and reduces sensitivity to changing circumstances, which is the opposite of what it promises to deliver.

This produces a self-sustaining loop: a bad mood makes a person less likely to do the things that would improve it, which then supplies fresh evidence for whatever the spiral is already arguing: that nothing helps, and that this is how things are now. Mood and behavior become locked together, and thinking harder about the mood, from inside the loop, tends to strengthen it rather than break it. Waiting to feel ready, in effect, means waiting on a signal that rumination is not designed to provide.

Why Reflection Might Still Help With a Negative Loop

None of this makes introspection the enemy. Psychologists distinguish between rumination and reflection: thinking that remains abstract and fixed on why something happened tends to spiral, while more concrete, distanced thinking about a problem tends to help. A 2022 meta-analysis published in Personality and Social Psychology Review, pooling more than two hundred studies, confirmed that both psychological distance and concrete processing reliably reduce the intensity of negative emotion.

One well-supported way to gain that distance is self-distancing: mentally stepping back and considering a situation the way an outside observer would, sometimes by coaching oneself by name. A 2021 study published in Clinical Psychological Science found that this kind of distanced self-talk reduced emotional reactivity across a range of experiences, including some of the most intense ones tested. Approached this way, reflection clarifies a problem rather than circling it.

article continues after advertisement

The relevant nuance is timing. Early in a spiral, when a mood has already narrowed attention and reduced motivation, action is the more accessible lever; it does not require the clarity that reflection demands. Reflection becomes more useful once there is already some distance, once a person has enough perspective to examine the problem rather than remain inside it. Attempting deep reflection while still fully submerged is often what keeps the analysis circling.

The deeper reason the small-action route works is that people are not purely cognitive beings who happen to have bodies attached. Mood, motivation, and physical action are closely linked, each capable of moving the others. That link cuts both ways. It is precisely what allows a bad mood to discourage the walk that would have helped. But it also means the loop can be entered from the behavioral side as easily as the emotional one. The underlying implication is that a person need not feel ready to begin. They only have to begin; readiness tends to follow.

That is a more forgiving way to think about a difficult stretch than most people allow themselves. It requires solving nothing. It requires one small, doable thing, done slightly before it feels justified.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: What I Learned After 16 Years of Kissing My Wife Wrong
item.description:
Sex

What I Learned After 16 Years of Kissing My Wife Wrong

For some men, kissing is just a step toward sex. For many women, it is the goal.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Once you start having sex, you don't really make out just to make out.
  • The wider the sensual playground, the richer the sexual experience.
  • It's in men's self-interest to cut the umbilical cord between kissing and sex.
  • Part of maturing as a man is moving from a hyper focus on sexuality to a wider focus on sensuality.
The wider the sensual, the richer the sexual.
Source: Shai Shachar, used with permission

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

For the past 16 years, Galit has told me from time to time that she doesn’t really enjoy the way I kiss. Not every time we kissed, but often enough that I noticed it. And I was like, sure, I’ll try. I guess it wasn’t that big of an issue for me.

She would also sometimes complain that she wanted more kissing, and that I don’t kiss her enough. She said I mostly kiss her when I want to have sex. I heard her, but I didn’t really change my oral lovemaking strategy.

Then a couple of months ago, toward the end of my 30-day challenge of touching Galit the way she wants to be touched, something changed. We were talking about kissing, and she laughed and said I don’t know how to make out, and that I haven’t made out since the ’90s.

I initially laughed, but then I got it. She’s right. Since I’ve started having sex, I’ve stopped investing in my smooching.

Once that penny dropped, I knew it was time to change. I decided to put my ego aside and try to explore kissing from her perspective. I took upon myself a new challenge. I decided I would kiss her every single day, the way she prefers, regardless of sex.

Where Do Boys Learn to Kiss?

As I embarked on this challenge, I began to unpack my core beliefs about kissing. I realized that for a lot of men, the conditioning is that kissing is just one step toward sex. The whole metaphor of making out that my generation grew up with was that of baseball: first base, second base, third base, home run. If kissing is first base, you don’t want to end up at first base. You want to get a home run.

Where did I learn how to kiss? No one ever really teaches you. I picked it up along the way, through movies, TV shows, porn, experiences, and my buddies telling me what to do. Part of my process was also realizing I never really saw my parents kiss. They had the mom-and-dad partner’s kiss. I never saw them kissing as lovers. So kissing for me was either not sensual at all or associated with sex.

The tipping point is that once you start having sex, you don’t really make out just to make out. Because after you scored a home run, you don’t really enjoy staying on first.

Sensual ≠ Sexual

What I learned from our previous touch challenge is that sensual doesn’t mean sexual. Sensual is meeting in the senses. Experiencing the lips, connecting the bodies, enjoying the smell, the heat, the energy. Sexual is one specific dimension of the sensual encounter. It only relates to sex, reproduction, and sexual organs. A much narrower definition.

article continues after advertisement

Sadly, many men conflate the two. From a young age, kissing gets categorized under the sexual, and not the sensual. It becomes associated with sex. Unfortunately, this has become the stigma: the horny husband who’s too tired for foreplay, hugging, or kissing, and just wants intercourse.

When kissing becomes linked to sex, the situation becomes binary. And binary thinking is not beneficial for relationships, and certainly not for sex. Especially for women. Many women share in the clinic that when their husbands kiss them, they already know that he’s looking for sex. That puts pressure on them. Pressure and sex don’t go together well. So it’s in men’s self-interest to cut the umbilical cord between kissing and sex.

Kissing Is a Portal

Long-term committed relationships require both, but in different ways. The goal of the sensual is to connect. To feel seen, to feel loved, to feel heard, to touch each other, to be connected. Sex is one means to that goal. Especially once you understand that there are actually two more ways to make love besides sex: mental and emotional.

So if men can learn to enjoy kissing for its own sake, they will unlock another gateway into the sensual. And the wider the sensual playground, the richer the sexual experience.

I believe that men want to be more sensual. We want to be celebrated, touched, and enjoyed. We’ve just been socialized that everything is about sex. If we dare to reframe kissing as a sensual opening, we will receive more love, attention, and caring from our partners.

As we age, our libido changes. Think about an elderly couple sitting next to each other on a bench, or in their wheelchairs. What they’ll probably enjoy is more sensuality, more connection, more touch, more kissing. That’s the good stuff.

Part of maturing as a man is moving from a hyper focus on sexuality to a wider focus on sensuality. More sensuality leads to a more satisfying and richer sexuality.

At the end of the day, what we really want is soul synergy, those rare moments that we transcend our existential loneliness, meet in a deepest way, and touch the sublime. Soul synergy happens when the physical, mental, and emotional lovemaking combine.

Kissing is not just part of physical lovemaking. It’s also an emotional move. It’s a way to be present together. When our bodies connect, when our lips join, when we’re exchanging that energy, we are making and transferring love. It’s just a different type of love.

article continues after advertisement

The Kissing Audit

So here’s our invitation: Kiss your partner every day the way they like, regardless of sex.

And if you dare, ask yourself: Where did you learn how to kiss? Then have an honest conversation with your partner about the kissing dynamic in your marriage.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: The Number-One Way Parents "Ruin" Adult Children's Lives
item.description:
Parenting

The Number-One Way Parents "Ruin" Adult Children's Lives

It's rarely the thing the parent thinks they did wrong.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Parents assume the "ruin" is a single traceable event, such as a divorce, a move, or a harsh word.
  • The real damage is almost never the event itself; it's the feeling that was never acknowledged.
  • Adult children don't want a re-litigation of facts; they want proof that someone finally understands them.

When an adult child says, “You ruined my life” (or some close version of that painful sentiment), most parents brace for a specific charge. Parents share with me how they scramble backward through decades, trying to locate the “crime.” The usual suspects that pop up in these parents’ minds may include: “Was it the divorce when she was nine?” Or, “What about when we moved, and he lost his friends?” “Oh, wait, I still don’t know what I was doing when I made that hurtful comment about her weight in tenth grade?”

This instinct to find the event is exactly what keeps parents stuck. That’s because the event isn’t really the point.

It Was Never About the Event

Parents, I have a new bulletin for you about the uncomfortable truth. The “ruining” that adult children describe to me is almost never about just what happened. It’s more about what happened afterward. By this I mean the years a feeling sat there, unnamed and unaddressed, while everyone moved on as if it hadn’t ever happened. For example, the divorce wasn’t the wound. The silence about how it felt to live inside it was. Or, that insensitive comment the parent made about her weight really hurt, but the minimization about that, even for years after, is what really festers the most in the adult child’s mind.

This is why parents so often “lose” these conversations even when they’re factually right. A father I coached insisted, quite accurately, that he never missed a single softball game. Yet his adult daughter isn’t lying when she says he wasn’t there.

How can this discrepancy exist, you may ask? Well, in this case, the daughter meant something else. That was that her father was present in the bleachers and absent when she needed him to notice she was struggling. Two true things, talking past each other.

Please don’t take this as me saying parents need to be perfect and not make mistakes. What I am saying, though, is that if you lead with curiosity to understand your adult child’s point of view, you will get a lot further than rigidly defending yourself. Further, you will model for them the power of understanding, hopefully inspiring them to extend that all-important caring courtesy to you as well.

The Debt Behind the Words

Once you see more than just your own point of view, the whole confrontation changes shape. The question stops being, “Did that even happen the way you’re describing?” and becomes, “What were you actually trying to tell me, then and now?” That single shift from defending the record to asking about the feeling is often the difference between a conversation that repairs something and one that just re-wounds everyone involved.

This is the territory I dig into in my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! I discuss that it is not about accepting blame you don’t deserve, but about understanding what adult children are actually asking for when they say those words. Spoiler: It’s rarely an apology for a fact. It’s an acknowledgment of a feeling that’s been left uncollected for years.

article continues after advertisement

Some Final Advice

So if you find yourself rehearsing your defense, the timeline, the evidence, the “but I was there,” then don’t keep doing that. Tempting as it is to keep wanting to come up with your “data’ to defend yourself the same fruitless way, say, “Enough of this, already,” to yourself. Instead, try pausing before you speak. Then gently ask, “What were you feeling back then that you never got to say out loud?” Or, “What did you say that I did not hear in the way that would have felt more supportive to you?”

You may find the debt your adult child thinks you owe isn’t the one you’ve been preparing to argue about at all. That’s not losing the argument, but instead, finally answering the right question.

item.title: The Secret to Success Wasn't Hidden—It Was Just Overlooked
item.description:
Intelligence

The Secret to Success Wasn't Hidden—It Was Just Overlooked

The most important predictor of success wasn't the one anyone expected.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Intelligence alone doesn't explain why some people achieve extraordinary success.
  • The questions you ask yourself during setbacks shape the paths you discover.
  • The mindset that drives long-term achievement can be intentionally developed.

For over 100 years, people have sought the key to success.

People built IQ tests to measure it. Schools built standardized tests to predict it. We have created an entire system for assigning value to grades, certifications, and talent, based on the belief that there is a simple formula for reaching your goals: The smarter you are, the more successful you will become.

It seems logical. But it is not the complete picture.

We all know someone who appeared destined for success but never quite achieved it, and we can also name someone who may not be the brightest person in the room but continues to succeed in ways that others do not.

One person sees the end of the road while the other sees a different path. That one difference changes everything.

The Missing Piece

Once it became clear that intelligence wasn’t the whole story, psychologists began searching for what was missing.

Maybe it is grit, willpower, or talent. Each has value, but none tells us what to do when the path we planned no longer exists.

The people who continue to grow seem to approach obstacles differently. They don't ask, Am I capable of overcoming this? Instead, they ask, What are some other ways I could solve this problem? The shift in questions changes the way someone thinks. It transforms a dead end into a detour. A setback into a strategy session. A failure into feedback.

Psychologists observed this pattern repeatedly but struggled to explain it. They could see that some people consistently found another path forward, yet they couldn't fully identify what separated them from everyone else. The answer, it turns out, wasn't another personality trait.

It was psychological hope.

The Discovery We Almost Missed

One of the most surprising findings in positive psychology, which sought to answer the question of who can solve problems in a study of school-age children, may have stumbled upon the answer. In the study, the researchers found that hope predicts academic achievement better than intelligence, personality, and previous academic performance (Day et al., 2010).

Read that again. Hope outperformed IQ. Not wishful thinking or blind optimism. Hope.

According to psychologist C. R. Snyder (2002), hope isn't just a feeling but a way of thinking that consists of two mental habits: believing you can reach your goals and believing you can find another path when obstacles appear.

article continues after advertisement

That second part matters. When hopeful people encounter setbacks, they don't ask, "Am I capable?" They ask, "What's another way?"

That question changes everything.

How to Create a More Hopeful Mind

The good news is that hope is not a constant; it’s malleable. It can grow. According to Snyder’s research on hope, it is built on two mental habits: believing you can reach your goals and believing you can find another way when obstacles appear. The stronger those habits become, the more likely you are to keep moving toward the future you want. (Snyder et al., 1991)

Fortunately, building hope doesn’t require changing who you are. It begins by changing how you think about your future and the obstacles that stand in your way. Here are three research-informed ways to begin strengthening your own hope level.

1. Picture Your Perfect Future

Don't simply think about who you want to become. Write it down in such incredible detail that it comes alive. Visualize yourself in ten years. Where will you be sleeping? Who will be with you? What do you do for work? How will you start each day? What will you have accomplished? How will you impact the lives of other people? Continue writing until what you have written about your future feels like it has happened.

The clearer you make your ultimate destination, the easier it will be for your mind to construct paths to your ultimate destination. Hope begins with a destination, and purpose gives people something meaningful to work toward (Bronk et al., 2009).

2. Act as That Person for Five Minutes

Rather than waiting until you are successful, act successful now. If you see your future self as a writer, then write for five minutes today. If you see your future self as a runner, download a running app and go for a walk around the block today. If you see your future self as being healthy, then prepare one healthy meal today.

Taking these small steps creates evidence of who you are. Evidence confirms your identity. Changing your identity can change how you act. Success does not come all at once but is built on thousands of small actions that are congruent with the person you want to be.

3. Reflect and Adjust

At the end of every day, ask yourself, “What did I do today to bring me closer to my ideal self?” Recognize and be grateful for your success. Then think about the barriers in your way and brainstorm three new ways to keep moving forward that leverage your strengths and talents.

article continues after advertisement

Often, we think we are stuck, but our brains are highly imaginative when we consider different options. Hopeful people do not run away from obstacles but rather create a new path around them. Sometimes the obstacle is not the dead end; it is pointing you in the direction of a better end.

The Secret Was Never Hidden

Hopeful people don’t succeed because they are smarter. They succeed because they refuse to see an obstacle as an ending. They imagine new possibilities. They take another step and keep going. Over time, those small decisions compound to create an extraordinary life.

The secret to success was never hidden.

We simply overlooked the power of a hopeful brain.

item.title: Placebo Effect: Mind Over Marijuana
item.description:
Placebo

Placebo Effect: Mind Over Marijuana

Can cannabis help us harness the healing effects of the mind?

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • There is evidence that placebos can treat pain and affect mood and immune response.
  • The endocannabinoid system (ECS) has been shown to be involved in delivering placebo-mediated analgesia.
  • The ECS appears to play a central role in creating homeostasis throughout the body.

The placebo effect has been part of medical conversation since the late 1700s, when an English physician named Dr. Alexander Sutherland coined the term to describe a doctor with an especially reassuring bedside manner. Today, the concept plays a central role in how we test new drugs: to prove a medication actually works, researchers have to compare it against a "dummy" pill or injection—something inert, with no active ingredient. Neither the patient nor the doctor is told which one the patient is getting, a setup called a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. This precaution exists because up to 40% of patients feel real, measurable benefits from a completely inactive treatment, simply because they believe it's the real thing.

When Belief Changes the Body

What's fascinating—and a little unsettling—is that over three centuries of medicine, we've learned that believing a treatment will help can cause the body to respond as if that treatment (proven or not) actually did. Studies have shown that a plain saltwater injection can ease pain, and a sugar pill can lower blood pressure.

I saw this firsthand during my medical residency. At the time, there was a common (and, I now think, troubling) practice: if a patient came in reporting pain and staff suspected they were exaggerating to get narcotics, we'd give them a shot of saline instead. If their pain went away, we took that as proof they hadn't really been in pain—they were just drug-seeking. Looking back after more than 40 years in medicine, I'm no longer confident that conclusion was right, and I've come to have real concerns about the ethics of that approach.

I'm not alone in thinking about this. A 2008 survey of nearly 700 physicians found that roughly half of internists and rheumatologists reported regularly prescribing placebo treatments, and most—62%—considered the practice ethically acceptable (1). In a separate, well-known study, 165 patients with knee arthritis underwent one of two real surgical procedures—or a fake surgery, where surgeons made incisions and went through the motions without actually treating anything. The results were no different across the groups (2). And in another striking experiment, Dr. Robert Ader showed that simply giving people a flavored drink could suppress their immune system if their body had been conditioned to associate that taste with an immune-suppressing drug (3).

Rethinking What's Actually Happening

Because of the ethical discomfort around deceiving patients with fake treatments, researchers have proposed better ways to describe what's really going on. One idea is the "meaning response"—the notion that healing is driven not just by a treatment's chemistry, but by the meaning, context, and ritual surrounding it: the doctor's confidence, the setting, the expectation of getting better. This same idea helps explain the flip side, called the nocebo effect, where a patient given an inactive substance but warned it might cause side effects actually experiences those side effects (4).

article continues after advertisement

Where Cannabis Comes In

We've long known that the body's own endorphin system—the same one responsible for a "runner's high"—plays a role in placebo pain relief. But a Swiss study looking at what happens in the brain during placebo pain relief found something else: the endocannabinoid system, or ECS, was involved too (5).

The ECS is a body-wide network of receptors and signaling molecules—related to, but distinct from, the compounds in cannabis—that helps regulate things like pain, mood, appetite, and immune response. It's part of how the body maintains balance, or homeostasis.

A 2017 study put this connection to the test directly. Twenty participants were told they'd be given a cannabis lollipop containing a high dose of THC (the main psychoactive compound in cannabis). In reality, they received an inactive version. Remarkably, many still experienced effects similar to genuine THC intoxication—the first study to show that people's expectations alone could produce a placebo "high" (6).

This lines up with something experienced practitioners in the cannabis and psychedelics field have long emphasized: set and setting—a person's mindset going in, and the environment they're in—can shape their response to a substance as much as the substance itself, alongside simple conditioning: your body learning to expect a certain effect (7).

A Physician's Perspective

Long before I specialized in cannabis medicine, I noticed something in the emergency room that I couldn't quite prove, but strongly suspected: keeping a calm, warm, humorous (when appropriate) presence with patients—even in the middle of treating serious, life-threatening conditions—seemed to genuinely improve how they did.

Years later, working as a cannabis physician and seeing the sheer range of conditions that cannabis seemed to help, I started paying closer attention to the ECS's central role in keeping the body in balance. Every organ system has cannabinoid receptors woven through it, tied into all sorts of regulatory processes. Watching patients respond to different cannabinoids—the well-known ones like THC and CBD, and lesser-known ones too—I began to wonder: could the ECS also be involved in the placebo effect itself, beyond just pain relief?

article continues after advertisement

The Open Question

Could there be a placebo-like benefit, driven by the ECS, in other conditions—Parkinson's disease (there are notably high concentrations of cannabinoid receptors in the brain regions Parkinson's affects), mood disorders, addiction, autoimmune illness, and more?

Here's where things stand: we know the ECS matters for all of these conditions in its own right. There's solid, independent evidence that ECS activity affects mood and anxiety, nausea, motor control in Parkinson's, and cravings related to addiction. What we don't yet have is the kind of study that would prove expectation and belief specifically recruit the ECS in these other conditions, the same way it appears to during pain relief—the equivalent of blocking a cannabinoid receptor and watching a placebo effect disappear. That experiment hasn't been done.

But there's no obvious reason it couldn't work that way. If the brain can tap into endocannabinoid signaling in response to expectation and conditioning for pain, it's reasonable to think it might do the same in other places where those same receptors show up and matter.

If that turns out to be true, it raises a compelling possibility: could doctors and patients learn to intentionally engage this system—this naturally occurring, ethical mind-body interaction—to support healing across a wide range of conditions, without needing to introduce any outside substance at all?

item.title: Presumed Intimate
item.description:
Trust

Presumed Intimate

Proximity isn't the same as trust—and boundaries can reveal the difference.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Closeness doesn’t guarantee trust, regardless of family, friend, or community status. Trust must be earned.
  • Boundaries don’t end relationships—they invite healthier possibilities for mutual recognition and growth.
  • Chosen family also requires trust maintenance. Lasting intimacy always depends on acts of mutual recognition.
Source: Linthicum, Richard. (from old catalog) / Wikimedia Commons

“But you’re family.”

“You’re best friends.”

“You’re so close.”

These are some of the reactions we hear when a relationship (as we know it) ends. It’s as if the appearance of closeness—the assigned role of family, “framily,” or friend—is enough to presume a deep intimacy between people, a trusting bond that is expected to withstand any rupture.

But proximity and trust are not the same thing.

The feeling of intimacy can be found quickly. People dive into the deep end of shared experiences, identities, and communities every day without a second thought. But true intimacy requires trust.

And research reveals that trust can’t be simply wished for, implied, or presumed. It must be earned continuously (Kelly, van der Werff, and Freeney, 2025).

One of my therapy clients, whom I’ll call Sasha, first discovered this distinction only after many years of presuming intimacy with her family of origin.

Sasha spent decades of her adulthood learning to set boundaries with her mother, father, and two brothers. She was never physically abused by them, but growing up she frequently experienced a damaging disruption to her process of finding and being herself. Whenever she expressed hurt, anger, disappointment, or desires that conflicted with those of her family members, she was made to feel guilty and ashamed for having those feelings in the first place.

A few of the statements she would hear, to keep her “in her place,” included:

“Other people have it worse.”

“At least you haven’t been kicked out of the house!”

“Get over yourself!”

Studies show that, like Sasha, many people who grow up in “good enough” families still experience chronic invalidation—if not gaslighting—that is damaging to their sense of self and relational trust (Kuo, Fitzpatrick, & Uliaszek, 2022). Instead of learning that their feelings matter and that they are worthy of being held in mind by others, they are taught that staying in the relationship (with family, friends, partners, a community) at all costs is what matters. And since “other people have it worse,” they are guilted into suffering in silence (Wang, Fang, and Pan, et al., 2026).

When Sasha became pregnant—years after learning to set boundaries with her family–she met another expectant mother at a yoga class. Their babies would be born weeks apart. Similar to Sasha, this new friend depended more on friends than family—in her case, she had a very small family of origin. Both women enjoyed the idea of raising their kids together, as they would share cultural heritage and both be racial minorities in a very White neighborhood. And so, they became inseparable overnight: “Framly,” as Sasha’s friend called it.

“It did feel like family, right away,” Sasha recalls. “And I realize now that this was exactly the problem.”

Much like with her family of origin, Sasha stopped asking herself a crucial question about her friend whenever she was invalidated by her: “Has this person earned my trust?”

Again, according to studies, trust must be earned and maintained consistently over time (Lewicki & Wiethoff, 2000).

When conflicts eventually arose between their kids, Sasha would consistently absorb the discomfort, worrying that speaking up could create a permanent rupture with her friend. And she feared losing her, as she felt like a lifeline to Sasha, a new parent finding her way. So Sasha convinced herself that in order to preserve the presumed intimacy with her friend, she would have to tolerate certain things about the friend’s parenting and her child’s behavior that compromised Sasha’s integrity.

Years into the friendship, when the children were in first grade, Sasha finally raised concerns about the other child’s behavior. Right away, the other mother became not only defensive but also positioned herself as a victim.

“You’ve hit me in a really specific way,” the friend said, in response to Sasha asking her to take note of how the friend’s son had been repeatedly breaking Sasha’s son’s toys.

The entire focus of the conversation quickly moved from Sasha’s concerns about the children to her friend’s hurt feelings. Accountability never came, and the friendship ended.

And furthermore, much like when Sasha set boundaries with her family, she now had to hear people in the community say things to her like: “But you two are so close? What could have happened? Surely you can just work it out.”

Many of us find ourselves asking the same questions when we witness or experience major ruptures in (presumably) intimate relationships—those that we believe should implicitly guarantee trust.

But, again: no relationship can guarantee trust. Trust must always be earned.

Along these lines, Sasha had to learn that boundaries are not punishments or threats; they are invitations. When we choose to set a boundary, we say to the other person, “You matter to me, this relationship matters to me. But we both need to feel safe here, and this is what I need to feel safe with you.”

By claiming our boundary, we instantly invite the other person to be curious about us, to work to repair the ruptures between us, and to take responsibility for their role in our relationship with them (Giacobbi and Lalot, 2025). Of course, they also have the option to double down on the idea that trust should be implied because of the nature of your relationship.

And if they choose the latter, then it is up to us to either submit to them and keep things as they are, or to take some space from them until they are ready to meet us halfway.

Many people—including those of us who are queer—have built chosen families because our families of origin refuse to recognize and acknowledge us (Zhang, Lawrence, Walters, Clark, Hanna-Walker, and Lefkowitz, 2022). And our chosen bonds can become profoundly intimate, nurturing, and even life–saving, a salvational second chance.

But even chosen family requires a trust that is earned through processes of recognition, accountability, and acknowledgment of one another’s needs.

No matter what intimate name we use to describe a relationship (family, chosen family, framily), trust can never be presumed or implied. Every relationship—whether with parents, siblings, spouses, or best friends—demands ongoing accountability for how we affect one another.

I often talk to clients about boundaries not as endings but as beginnings. Not as a destructive pushing away, but as a creative process like pruning a garden. Right after you’ve pruned, the garden looks sparse, perhaps even empty or lonely. It can seem like you may have destroyed something beautiful, for good. But, as studies on boundary-setting and post-traumatic growth show us, pruning isn’t an act of destruction or an ending. It’s an act of creation, a beginning, an invitation for healthier and more sustaining growth (Tedeschi, Moore, and Greene, 2025).

This was Sasha’s experience. The end of one deeply enmeshed friendship left her grieving for a while—and this triggered the original grief she experienced with her family years before. But it also created room for mutually recognizing relationships in which her feelings were celebrated and not shut down, dismissed, or minimized. Her immediate chosen family became smaller for a season, but soon enough, it became richer and more abundant than she’d ever imagined.

Trust isn’t proven by the presumption or expectation for a certain kind of relationship—be it family, best friends, or romantic partnership. Trust is proven by how each person shows up with one another, how they are each challenged, and how they adapt in order to genuinely see and be seen, and to hear and be heard.

item.title: They Kept Me Safe, But They Never Knew Me
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

They Kept Me Safe, But They Never Knew Me

Personal Perspective: A broken mind needs continuity to heal.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Continuity and relationship aren't extras added to psychiatric treatment; they are the treatment.
  • When a care team belongs to the unit rather than the patient, clinicians change with your geography.
  • Hospitals built for safety and stabilization can process a mind without ever coming to know it.
  • Families are often the only continuous thread in a patient's care, yet the system gives them no way in.
Source: Gabino De Oro/Unsplash

I spent four months in a county jail before a court accepted my plea of not guilty by reason of mental disease. The finding placed me in the custody of the state instead of a prison, and for the next 10 months I was a patient at a state psychiatric hospital. After the jail, it felt like a pardon. Here, at last, was something that looked like care: a psychiatrist who led a weekly meeting, a psychologist, a social worker, an occupational therapist, a nurse, a whole team convened around my recovery. On paper, it was an enviable model.

It took me a while to understand why it so rarely felt that way.

The Team That Belonged to the Unit

The hospital's organizing principle was safety. Not understanding. Safety. Almost everything else followed after that.

The most consequential design flaw was one I did not notice at first: the treatment team belonged to the unit, not to the patient. The hospital was arranged as a ladder of security levels, and as you climbed or slipped, you changed units, and your team changed with you. Each unit held around 20 men whose faces and diagnoses rotated constantly. No one stayed beside you long enough to know you.

I learned what that cost through a loss I still feel. On one unit I had begun acceptance and commitment therapy with a psychologist I trusted, and for a few months it was doing something real: I was learning to sit with my own mind instead of fighting it. Then I changed units. My new psychologist practiced a different model entirely. The relationship was gone, and the therapy's through-line with it. I did not resume where I had stopped. I started over.

You could feel the same rupture in the medicine. My regimen was altered three times in two months: an antipsychotic raised, then lithium introduced as the "gold standard," then doses chased toward therapeutic levels, all by clinicians who, through no fault of their own, lacked the time to know me well enough to know what I needed. It had the paperwork of a treatment plan and the logic of a guess. In a state institution stretched to its margins, safety had become the whole of care. Feeling, connection, the slow labor of understanding a particular human being—these were luxuries the model could not afford. Safety trumped the beating heart.

T. M. Luhrmann has described American psychiatry as split between two ways of treating a mind: managing it biochemically, and understanding it as a person. Understanding takes time no one on that ward had. Norah Vincent, who committed herself to psychiatric wards and wrote about it in Voluntary Madness, concluded that such places were never built to heal the sick; they were built to spare the well the sight of them.

Source: Ardalan Hamedani/Pexels

There was one person who could have supplied the continuity the system could not: my mother. She had known me for decades. She could have told any team what I looked like when I was well, what my warning signs were, what a medication was doing that no chart could show. She asked to be part of my care. There was no mechanism for it. A stretched institution has no place at its table for a family member who wants to help; the one thread running through every unit was treated as an interruption instead of a resource. The hospital would say, correctly, that it lacked the resources. That is the point: the continuity a recovering mind depends on had been classed as a luxury.

Continuity is not a nicety layered on top of psychiatric treatment. For a broken mind, continuity is the treatment. Healing happens inside a sustained relationship: someone who knew you last week and will know you next week, who can tell the difference between the real you and the symptom, who is there when the medication is changed again. A system that cannot keep the same people beside you cannot, in any deep sense, treat you. It can only stabilize you and pass you along.

What It Costs to Be Processed

I was stable the entire time I was in that hospital, and I want to be fair about what that was worth: it kept me safe, and I am grateful I did not come apart again. But I was kept, not known. I held together in a place that watched me without knowing me—alone, essentially, among people paid to observe me.

To be processed by a system built for safety is to become a case rather than a person. You are stabilized without being understood. You get better on paper while remaining, to nearly everyone around you, a stranger who is behaving well. Marie Balter, who spent years wrongly institutionalized and later returned to work in the field, asked whether anyone in it would take real risks for the patients others had given up on. Most days, the answer the building gave was no. Not out of malice; the people there were mostly decent and overwhelmed. It was the design that left them no room to know me.

There is a particular loneliness in recovering under observation—in doing the hardest work of your life surrounded by people whose job is to record your behavior. What I needed, and what almost no institution is built to provide, was not more watching and not another medication trial. It was continuity. It was to be known, steadily, by someone who would still be there tomorrow.

My stability did not change after my release; my life did. It grew fuller among the people who stayed: who learned my illness alongside me, who chose again and again to remain. That is what the hospital could not manufacture, and what no amount of safety can replace. A place can keep a mind from harm and never come close to healing it. We have built institutions that can stabilize a person without ever knowing one, and then we have called the result care.

It is worth asking what psychiatric care might look like if it were organized to accompany a person through the worst thing that has ever happened to them, rather than to manage the risk they pose. It would be slower. It would cost more. It would keep the same faces in the room. And it might, at last, deserve the name.

item.title: Moving Beyond Impostor Syndrome: Introducing Impostorization
item.description:
Imposter Syndrome

Moving Beyond Impostor Syndrome: Introducing Impostorization

What if your self-doubt isn't impostor syndrome but impostorization?

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Impostor syndrome refers to feelings of inadequacy that people experience despite a pattern of achievement.
  • Steps to conquer impostor syndrome take a fix-the-individual approach (i.e., confidence training, power pose).
  • Discussions on impostor syndrome assume the person is the problem. But what if it is really the environment?
  • Impostorization refers to the systems, interactions, and dynamics that trigger impostor feelings.

We have probably heard or read about impostor syndrome—those feelings of inadequacy that people experience and the fear that others will discover they do not belong in the position they occupy. What is problematic about the discussions, articles, and social media clips on impostor syndrome is that they assume the person is the problem.

The narrative goes something like this.

Are you feeling incompetent? Do you feel like you do not belong in your position or the university you got into?

If so, then you are experiencing impostor syndrome. The advice, which may include strengthening your self-esteem or standing in power poses, often takes a fix-the-individual approach.

But what if these feelings of unintelligence and unbelonging are not stemming from within but rather from the environments we occupy? What if these feelings are being triggered by the workplaces, universities, and other spaces we are in?

Source: Ann H / Pexels

The external factors that may elicit the feelings typically labeled impostor syndrome are what I call impostorization.

Impostorization refers to the policies, practices, and seemingly harmless interactions in an environment that can make (or attempt to make) us question our intelligence, competence, and sense of belonging.

I wish I could say that I magically produced a term to describe the systems and processes that make us feel like impostors, but I did not. The word came to me after delivering one of the most humiliating presentations of my career.

Yes, you read that correctly. Humiliating.

I had been hired to deliver a one-hour presentation on impostor syndrome to a large audience of entrepreneurs. I started by defining the term, and as I progressed to my second slide, a participant raised his hand and noted, “I understand what you are describing, but this does not apply to me.” Another participant echoed the sentiment shortly thereafter.

There I was, standing before a sea of entrepreneurs who nodded in agreement as the two participants spoke. It was painfully obvious that my presentation would be of little relevance to this audience.

What would you have done if you were me?

I looked at my watch and had 55 minutes left of content that would be of little to no value to my audience. I wanted to simply end the session and rush to the airport to catch the fastest flight home.

But I did not.

Feeling defeated, I closed my presentation and stood there for a few seconds. I then mustered the courage to ask the audience to help me understand what they had experienced.

For the next 50-plus minutes, I simply listened.

Dozens shared accounts of investors, family members, and others who questioned their expertise and their ability to succeed as an entrepreneur. They expressed their frustration and disappointment that so many people doubted them.

Despite having the right skills and experience, they were questioned and made to feel as though they were not as competent as they believed. Some managed to stay the course, while others said that this external doubt shook their belief and they now wondered whether they should quit.

It was then that I realized that what this audience was describing was not an issue stemming from within but rather, stemming from the outside.

After replaying in my mind the experiences and insights that the audience shared, I understood that impostor syndrome did not capture their lived experiences.

That night, I did not get much sleep. I tossed and turned as I tried to come up with a term that would capture their accounts. I also thought about my own personal and professional experiences and all the time I and others labeled my feelings impostor syndrome and assumed it was a “me-issue.” I remember being in environments where I felt I did not belong. I remember feeling unqualified to serve in positions despite having the necessary experience and degrees.

Then it occurred to me that while individuals may indeed experience impostor syndrome, there are also people who are made to feel like they are impostors. Impostorization became the term used to describe the external environment, biases, and systemic practices—rather than internal factors or personality traits—that trigger impostor feelings.

Impostorization occurs in universities, workplaces, relationships, families, and society.

This article is intended as an introduction to impostorization. Drawing on extant research, interviews, and my personal experiences, I will write in the future about impostorization across different contexts and how we can counter its effects.

item.title: News Anxiety? Stop Listening to One Type of Story
item.description:
Anxiety

News Anxiety? Stop Listening to One Type of Story

Facts and analysis inform you. Speculation makes you anxious.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • The 24-hour news cycle fills extra time with speculation.
  • Because the economic realities of the media is that we click when we're scared, speculation skews frightening.
  • Focusing on concrete facts and analysis that provides context provides information without feeding anxiety.

When consuming news makes us anxious, we’re often told to stop following the news. But that is not the answer. The answer is to choose the type of news you consume.

Rural Areas Can Be Cell Phone Deserts

I am in the midst of a three week camping trip – visiting family, tramping on beaches, and playing the banjo. We have moved from backpacking to "tiny teardrop" – a trailer with two doors opening on a mattress and an outside kitchen you access through the trunk. I do love power and water though – and nowhere we’ve camped so far has either. Our solar panels keep this iPad, our phones, and my husband’s hearing aids charged and the sink and fan running. But cell service is thin on the ground and my portable satellite link requires more power than I want to risk after three days of clouds and rain.

So I’m feeling great! And my husband is feeling even better. Why? No news.

Three Types of News

Like many folks, the constant torrent of events had kept me scanning the news, waiting for the next event that will rock the world.

Then I made an important observation about my mental well-being: some news kept me informed. Most news just made me anxious. There’s a reason for that. Two actually: the 24-hour news cycle and the fact that we are wired to watch for danger. News alerts us to danger.

Analyzing my own (constant) intake of news, I identified 3 types of stories:

  • Factual accounts of events. A prime minister resigns. A city is bombed. Peace talks are underway. These stories tell us WHAT happened.
  • Analysis of events. These stories break down current and past events and gives us insight into WHY things happened. For example, the Supreme Court makes a decision and an analyst tells us the background information, what legal precedents were drawn on, and what the broader implications of the case are for the future.
  • Speculation about what might happen in the future. These stories involve analysts arguing about what is happening now and how they might play out in the future. AI will bring in a utopia where drudgework is done by machines vs. AI will throw all of us out of work. AI will cause our brains to rot as we wallow in slop, and we will become puppets who can do manual labor.

I’m sure you’ve read those stories.

As the demand for news has risen and the financial model for news sources has increasingly relied on clicks, there have been two changes in what we are offered:

  • There is more and more speculative analysis. Why? It is always easy to get an expert to talk and it does not rely on an actual event to occur. You can always do it.
  • The analysis skews scary. We seek out information when we’re frightened.
article continues after advertisement

News Anxiety and the Stoic Response

Although there are many types of anxiety, free-floating general anxiety – like the kind generated by consuming too much news – is a feeling that we are in danger. That danger can come from anywhere: our safety is at risk; our reputation is at risk; our loved ones or things we care about are at risk. Some people are more anxious than others, but for all of us, anxiety is exacerbated when we feel we don’t know what is happening, why it’s happening, or how to stop it. We naturally want to protect ourselves and our loved ones from danger. One way to do that is to get more information.

Stoicism is a philosophical approach to help people cope with the fact that bad things happen. We lose people we care about. We are hurt. We don’t get what we want. Stoicism is a method for coping with the anxiety that this produces.

Core elements of Stoic practice include:

  • Looking at what is happening and acknowledging that which we can change and that which we cannot.
  • When we have control and can change things, we can work to make more positive things happen and to stop negative things.
  • When things are out of our control, we acknowledge and accept that. We also acknowledge that we can control how we respond to the world.
  • Working to foster virtue within ourselves.

How Stoicism Changed My Relationship to the News

I aspire to practice Stoicism. I am also a news hound. A few months ago, I realized all this news consumption was helping my anxiety spiral:

  • The more news I consumed, the more anxious I got.
  • The more anxious I got, the more I felt threatened and that the world was a dangerous place.
  • The more danger I perceived, the more I sought out information.

News made me feel the world was dangerous. I got anxious. I consumed more news.

So I stopped. Because this is something I can control.

I continue to read factual accounts of what is happening in the world. Knowledge is critical for an informed citizenry and for me personally. I know to tell my kids to check their federal loan accounts, how scientific funding for psychology is at risk, and how to protect myself from seasonal ticks.

article continues after advertisement

I also follow analysis of important events so I can better understand my world. If I know why things happen, I can better understand what is important for me to act on (ticks, nutrition, loans), and what is beyond my power to change. It helps me know where to put my energy and how to protect myself and those I love.

But I’ve almost stopped reading speculation about what is going to happen. The most critical aspects of future impacts are covered in standard news analysis. The rest is guesswork. All that type of article does is tell you all about the many things that might happen but haven’t yet.

(I also read positive fun news about dogs, space, art, literature, and good things that people still do to make the world a better place.)

And you know what? My anxiety cycle went through the floor. I felt informed. I could focus my actions. And I didn’t feel scared and out of control all of the time.

A Final Experiment

In our travels, we’ve barely had cell service, and even then only on the road and only enough for Google Maps or Waze. My anxiety hasn’t changed. But my husband’s has gone through the floor.

Why? No news.

He loves podcasts where experts argue about the dire consequences of every current event.

Those podcasts say almost nothing about what we can do. All about outrage and HELPLESS INEVITABILITY.

With that noise from speculative analysis gone, his anxiety shrank as well.

Now there is an action that he has control of.

item.title: Can You Trust Your Desire?
item.description:
Mating

Can You Trust Your Desire?

Why your body, heart, and mind don't always want the same thing.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Attraction begins before conscious thought.
  • Desire arises from multiple inner systems.
  • The body, heart, and mind can want different things.
Source: AI-Generated

Several years ago, a friend described a two-week vision quest in the desert. As he spoke, I noticed something unusual unfolding inside me. Although I still knew very little about the experience and had not yet considered the practical implications, another part of me had already arrived at a conclusion. Before my rational mind had gathered enough information to make an informed decision, something deeper seemed to whisper, Yes. You need to do this.

The experience stayed with me long after the conversation ended, not because I eventually joined the retreat, but because it raised a question that extends far beyond spiritual journeys. It is the same question many of us encounter when we unexpectedly fall in love, feel an irresistible attraction, or discover ourselves drawn toward something or someone who seems to bypass our careful reasoning.

Where does desire actually come from?

For centuries, poets have described attraction as magic, destiny, fate, or chemistry. Psychologists have offered different explanations, pointing to biology, attachment, learning, and unconscious processes. While each perspective captures an important piece of the puzzle, I have come to believe that the more interesting question is not whether desire originates in the body, the mind, or the heart, but whether these different parts of ourselves are speaking with one voice. If they are not, and clinical experience suggests they rarely are, then another set of questions naturally follows. Which of these voices deserves our attention? Can we influence them, or are we simply passengers carried along by forces beyond our awareness?

Attraction Begins Before Conscious Thought

Many people assume they consciously choose whom they find attractive. In reality, attraction usually begins long before conscious thought enters the picture. Within moments of meeting another person, the brain and nervous system have already evaluated hundreds of subtle signals, including facial expressions, body language, vocal tone, scent, emotional presence, confidence, familiarity, and countless other cues that never reach conscious awareness.

Only after these rapid unconscious processes have taken place does the thinking mind begin constructing an explanation. We tell ourselves that we appreciate someone's intelligence, kindness, confidence, or sense of humor, yet these explanations often emerge after the initial attraction has already been established. In many ways, consciousness functions less like the architect of desire and more like its narrator, creating a coherent story about feelings that have already begun to emerge.

This understanding helps explain why attraction may feel mysterious. We often experience ourselves as making deliberate choices when, in reality, our nervous system has already made an initial assessment based upon years of accumulated experiences, implicit memories, biological predispositions, and attachment patterns.

Recognizing that attraction begins unconsciously does not mean we lack free will. It simply reminds us that awareness usually follows experience rather than precedes it.

We Have Multiple Desires

One of the greatest misconceptions about romantic attraction is the belief that desire is singular. We often speak as though there is one authentic voice within us waiting to be discovered, and that happiness depends upon learning to follow it. Yet, reality suggests something far more nuanced.

Human beings are composed of multiple biological and psychological systems, each shaped by evolution to serve a different function and each operating according to its own internal logic. Our body may respond to vitality, sexuality, physical attraction, and instinctive chemistry. Our heart longs for emotional safety, acceptance, intimacy, and love. Our rational mind evaluates character, compatibility, shared values, integrity, and the practical realities of building a life together.

These systems are not inherently in conflict, yet they often pull us in different directions. A person may ignite tremendous physical chemistry while repeatedly undermining emotional security. Another individual may offer warmth, stability, and kindness without awakening the same level of passion. Still another may appear ideal according to every rational standard while failing to evoke any emotional connection at all.

When people tell me they feel confused about their relationships, I rarely assume they are confused. More often, different parts of them express different desires.

When Desire Becomes Misleading

Understanding that attraction begins unconsciously also helps explain why desire is not always an accurate guide. Individuals who grew up with inconsistency, emotional distance, or unpredictability may later experience those same qualities as exciting because they unconsciously resemble early attachment experiences. What feels like chemistry can sometimes be the activation of unfinished emotional patterns rather than the beginning of genuine intimacy.

This distinction is especially important because our culture frequently romanticizes intensity. We speak of being swept off our feet, falling head over heels, or feeling unable to stop thinking about someone. While these experiences may accompany healthy love, they can also emerge when unresolved attachment wounds are activated. Emotional intensity should therefore never be mistaken for emotional compatibility.

Similarly, the absence of overwhelming excitement does not necessarily indicate the absence of love. Secure relationships often develop more gradually, allowing trust, emotional safety, and admiration to deepen over time. They may feel quieter than infatuation, yet they frequently provide a stronger foundation for enduring intimacy.

Listening Without Surrendering

People often ask whether they should trust their gut, follow their heart, or rely on reason. I believe the question itself is incomplete because it assumes only one of these systems deserves to lead. Psychological maturity involves something far more demanding. It requires learning to listen carefully to each voice without allowing any single voice to dominate the conversation.

Our body provides invaluable information about attraction, vitality, and emotional resonance. Our heart alerts us to our longing for closeness, belonging, and connection. Our rational mind contributes judgment, foresight, and the ability to evaluate long-term compatibility. Even our protective parts deserve compassion because they often developed in response to genuine experiences of hurt or disappointment.

The goal is therefore not to silence these different voices but to help them work together. Healthy decision-making emerges when instinct, emotion, reflection, and values gradually become aligned rather than competing for control.

Desire Is a Compass

Throughout my professional work, I have often described emotions as a compass rather than a dictator. I believe the same principle applies to desire. Like every emotion, desire is less interested in giving us instructions than in revealing our needs, our values, our history, and the direction in which we long to grow.

Attraction deserves our attention because it reveals something meaningful about our needs, longings, values, and history. Yet it should never be mistaken for a command that must be obeyed.

Ignoring desire can disconnect us from ourselves, but blindly following every attraction can disconnect us from wisdom. The healthiest relationships emerge not because we suppress our impulses or surrender to them unquestioningly, but because we become increasingly capable of understanding what those impulses are trying to communicate.

Perhaps the deepest challenge in romantic relationships is not deciding whether to trust the body, the heart, or the mind. It is developing enough self-awareness to recognize when these different parts are speaking, understanding what each contributes, and patiently helping them move toward greater harmony. When attraction, emotional security, personal values, and thoughtful reflection begin to harmonize, desire no longer feels like an uncontrollable force. Instead, it becomes what it was always meant to be: a guide that points us toward connection while leaving the final decision in our hands.
